questions.q:
can you help me answer this or tell me who might be a good member to reach out to? For Ian, I'll throw out one big Amazon challenge, with absolutely no expectation that anyone can solve it, because I believe it's a systemic Amazon problem that many sellers experience. But if anyone here has a solution, I will gleefully pay your membership dues!
Some background: EZ Outlet created a brand-new product category of hard-bodied electrical outlet extenders (wall power). Because these products carry household electrical current, we invested significant time and money to become safety certified by Intertek, a Nationally Recognized Testing Laboratory (NRTL). We're certified to UL 498A, 1363, 1310, and 62368-1 — standards that require components inside the product to be certified as well. Building a truly safety-certified outlet extender costs far more than building one that isn't, which makes our product the most expensive in the marketplace. As far as we know, we're also the only truly safety-certified brand in the category.

Success brought an onslaught of copycats that imitate our look and function but carry no safety certification whatsoever. Many are downright dangerous — three-prong outlets with no actual ground wire inside, for example. Yet Amazon doesn't require products in this category to submit NRTL documentation proving they're safety certified.

Consumers assume Amazon wouldn't allow uncertified electrical products on its marketplace, so it never occurs to them to check. Standing between our $49.95 certified extender and a $34.95 uncertified lookalike, they can't tell the difference, and they buy the cheaper one. Cheap foreign-made knockoffs have now overtaken us in volume, and we're no longer the leader in the very category we established. There's also a recourse problem: we're an American company that consumers can actually reach if something goes wrong. The foreign sellers behind these unsafe knockoffs are nearly impossible to contact in the event of an electrical safety incident; consumers are left with no recourse at all.

I believe the real solution is for Amazon to police safety certifications in categories like ours, requiring NRTL documentation before a listing can go live. Aside from it being the right thing to do for consumers to enforce this, it would probably also triple our current Amazon business as I think we are the only brand that passes safety testing.
